People who took a twenty-minute walk after their evening meal fell asleep faster and woke less often during the night than those who stayed on the sofa, according to a small trial carried out at the Fairhaven Institute for Sleep Research.

The researchers recruited 96 adults aged between 35 and 70 who said they often struggled to get to sleep. For four weeks, half of them were asked to walk at a comfortable pace for twenty minutes, starting within an hour of finishing dinner. The other half kept to their usual evening routine.

Everyone wore a wrist sensor at night and kept a short sleep diary each morning. By the end of the trial, the walking group were falling asleep about eleven minutes faster on average than at the start, while the comparison group showed almost no change.

The walkers also reported waking fewer times during the night, and they rated their sleep as more refreshing. The differences in total sleep time between the two groups were small, however, and the authors say that more work is needed before drawing firm conclusions.

"We think a few things are going on at once," said Dr Tobias Wren, who led the study. "Gentle movement helps the body handle the sugar from a meal, it gets people away from bright screens for a while, and many of our walkers simply enjoyed the routine. Any of those could make it easier to wind down later."

Sleep specialists not involved in the work welcomed the findings but urged caution. The trial was short, the participants knew which group they were in, and wrist sensors are less precise than the laboratory equipment used in larger studies.

Still, the advice is easy to follow and carries little risk. The researchers suggest keeping the pace gentle, since hard exercise late in the evening can have the opposite effect, and walking outside where possible, even after dark, rather than on a treadmill in front of a television.
